title: Short Stuff: Bird Migration
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry sitting in for Dave) cover bird migration in this Short Stuff episode, drawing on a HowStuffWorks article by Aliyah Hoyt and an interview with Dr. Andrew Farnsworth of the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. They explain migratory restlessness and photoperiod, obligate versus facultative migrants, how far birds travel (from short altitude shifts to pole-to-pole Arctic Tern journeys), the bar-tailed godwit's record nonstop flight from Alaska to New Zealand, and how birds navigate using landmarks, stars, the sun, and possibly Earth's magnetic field. The episode closes with a tangent about X-ray glasses and sensing magnetic fields, and a digression on a Ricky Gervais "Extras" scene and the film Zapped.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to bird migration
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic after seeing a V-shaped flock of birds, noting that not all birds fly south. He introduces migratory restlessness and photoperiod, and the two categories of migrants: obligate and facultative.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break in the episode before returning to the main discussion.

segments.title: Obligate versus facultative migrants
segments.summary: The hosts explain that obligate migrants are hardwired and predictable, while facultative migrants respond to cues such as food supply or cold. They compare facultative migrants to surfers.

segments.title: How far birds migrate
segments.summary: Dr. Andrew Farnsworth of the Cornell Lab of Ornithology says distances vary: some birds shift altitude on a mountain, some move within a state, and some travel pole to pole. The Arctic tern's round trip is close to 19,000 miles, the longest animal migration. The bar-tailed godwit holds the record for a nonstop flight from Alaska to New Zealand.

segments.title: Bird navigation and destinations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss where birds go and how they find their way. Some birds return to the same places and follow landmarks. Birds may use constellations, the sun, and possibly Earth's magnetic field, with a theory that some birds have a pigment that lets them see it.

segments.title: Tangent on seeing magnetic fields and X-ray glasses
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck speculate about future technology that could let people see magnetic fields or UV, joking about X-ray glasses. They then digress into a Ricky Gervais and Patrick Stewart scene from Extras and the 1980s film Zapped.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh closes the episode and the show's production credit is read.
